observation: Bulk data replication across multiple cloud regions and providers is essential for data analytics, disaster recovery, and geo-distributed model serving, yet cloud multicast can be expensive due to per-GB network egress fees and slow due to cloud network constraints. Egress prices vary by up to 23× across region pairs, with intra-cloud egress costing $0.01–$0.19 per GB and inter-cloud egress costing $0.08–$0.23 per GB, and cross-region bandwidth varies by up to 202×. Cloud providers impose per-VM egress/ingress limits (for example, AWS throttles egress to 5 Gbps per VM), so a single source VM is often the bottleneck, while users must still meet target replication times. Existing throughput-oriented multicast optimizers do not handle monetary cost, and existing cost-aware multicast work either ignores throughput or assumes a capacity-based pricing model that is inconsistent with today's per-GB egress pricing.

claims: Application-layer multicast builds overlay trees or meshes to deliver data to many receivers and optimizes the overlay for aggregate throughput or end-to-end delay rather than monetary cost.
Throughput-centric overlay multicast does not model the egress fees that clouds charge when traffic leaves a region or a provider.
Peer-assisted file dissemination protocols deliberately engage the upload bandwidth of multiple helper nodes so that a single source VM is not the throughput bottleneck.

claims: Minimum-cost multicast with network coding is formulated over capacitated links in which each link has a cost per unit of carried rate, and the task is to find a minimum-cost subgraph for a fixed multicast rate.
This capacity-based cost model is inconsistent with per-byte egress fees that vary by destination region and provider, and it does not decide throughput jointly with cost.

works.title: Minimum-Cost Multicast over Coded Packet Networks

claims: Geo-distributed analytics schedulers incorporate monetary cost into their data-placement and query-routing decisions.

Those schedulers are scoped to repeated analytical queries and do not address one-time bulk replication of large datasets to a user-specified set of cloud regions and providers under per-VM bandwidth caps and per-GB charges.

works.title: Iridium: Fast and Cheap Analytics for Wide-Area Data

solution.idea: The key obstacle is that existing systems optimize the wrong objective or use the wrong cost model. Throughput-oriented overlay multicast and peer-assisted dissemination (End System Multicast, SplitStream, Bullet, Overcast, FastReplica) deliberately engage many helper nodes to remove the source VM bottleneck, but they treat all links as equally desirable and ignore that each region/provider pair has a per-GB egress fee. On the other hand, minimum-cost coded multicast (Lun) handles the topology economics but was formulated for capacity-priced links with a fixed multicast rate; it does not reflect that egress is charged per byte actually transferred and it does not jointly decide how fast data must move to meet a user deadline. Geo-distributed schedulers such as Iridium are scoped to repeated analytics queries, not a one-time bulk replication to an arbitrary receiver set. The direction I choose is therefore to cast one-time bulk replication as a deadline-constrained, cost-minimizing multicasting problem on a directed overlay graph, where each directed edge is labeled by the real per-GB egress fee and by the achievable bandwidth, and each VM is labeled by its per-VM egress cap. Because the fee is per byte, the monetary cost over the entire replication is linear in the total number of bytes carried on each edge, independent of how those bytes are spread across time. The deadline then appears only through the required multicast rate R = file_size / deadline and through the fact that bandwidth capacities limit how many bytes an edge or a VM can carry within that time. This gives a single, clean mathematical formulation: choose per-edge transmission rates so that every target VM can receive at rate R for T seconds, respecting edge bandwidth limits and per-VM aggregate caps, while minimizing total egress cost. Network coding, as in Lun's minimum-cost coded multicast, is the right building block because it sidesteps the need to pack disjoint overlay trees; each VM can store, code, and forward partial information, and the feasibility constraint is a linear cut constraint rather than a combinatorial tree-packing condition. I further borrow the peer-assisted idea from FastReplica: to avoid making one original source VM the sole bottleneck, we allow several seed VMs in the source region to hold the initial copy; the optimizer then treats them all as equivalent sources and distributes outgoing duties among them. The main design trade-off is between a distributed, measurement-driven overlay that adapts over time and a centralized, model-driven optimizer that takes a snapshot of prices and bandwidths. The former is more robust to bandwidth variability but cannot guarantee a global optimum; the latter gives a reproducible optimum but needs accurate inputs. I choose the centralized optimizer because bulk datasets are large, target regions are known in advance, and the egress price matrix is stable. Another alternative is to solve the problem by greedily selecting a single overlay tree per chunk; this fails to capture sharing of edge capacities among chunks and leads to high cost. The proposed coded formulation avoids this by optimizing all edge rates jointly and simultaneously handles monetary cost, per-VM caps, and the deadline.
solution.implementation:
The implementation has three components: graph construction, optimization, and dissemination.

1. Inputs and graph. Let F be the dataset size in bytes and T the target replication deadline in seconds. Define the node set V to include every mandatory target VM plus one or more seed VMs that already contain the full dataset at the source region (local copies, if needed, so that the original source bottleneck is multiplied). For every ordered pair of distinct VMs (u,v), obtain: egress price E(u,v) in dollars per GB charged when u transfers to v; achievable bandwidth B(u,v) in bytes/sec from u to v; per-VM outgoing cap out(u) in bytes/sec. Construct a directed graph with variables r_{u,v} >= 0, the average rate (bytes/sec) of the coded transfer from u to v over the replication interval. If a transfer is impossible, set B(u,v)=0.

2. Optimization model. The objective is to minimize the total egress spend, which over a fixed T is proportional to sum_{u,v} E(u,v) r_{u,v}. Feasibility constraints are: (a) rate bound r_{u,v} <= B(u,v); (b) per-VM aggregate outgoing bound sum_v r_{u,v} <= out(u) for every u; (c) optional per-VM ingress bound sum_u r_{u,v} <= in(v); (d) multicast cut constraints. Let R = F/T. For every terminal t and every subset S of VMs that contains a seed and does not contain t, require sum_{u in S, v not in S} r_{u,v} >= R. These are exactly the min-cut conditions for a network-coded multicast of rate R; they are necessary and sufficient when forwarding VMs use random linear network coding. This is a linear program with exponentially many cut constraints. Solve it by cut generation: start with only (a)-(c) and nonnegativity; solve the LP; for each terminal t, compute the maximum flow from the seed side to t in the graph whose edge capacities are the current r_{u,v}; if any of those values is below R, find the corresponding min cut and add its inequality; repeat until no violated cut exists. If no feasible solution exists, the target T is too aggressive; to produce an achievable plan, run a binary search on T (equivalently on R) to find the smallest feasible deadline and the associated min-cost rates.

3. Dissemination schedule. The LP solution gives a per-edge rate r_{u,v}, which is also the amount of data that must traverse edge (u,v) over T. To realize it on a real cloud without requiring all edges to start transmitting simultaneously from time 0, I adapt the FastReplica peer-assisted pattern. Split the dataset into N fixed-size packets. The seed VMs first perform a bootstrap phase: each seed sends a disjoint subset of the packets to the first-hop relays that appear in its outgoing solution, using only the rates chosen by the LP. As soon as a relay has received at least one packet, it begins sending on its own outgoing edges at the LP-computed rates. After bootstrap, all VMs continue in steady state using random linear network coding: every VM stores packets it has received and transmits coded linear combinations on each outgoing edge at the rate r_{u,v}; because the underlying coded-flow solution satisfies the cut constraints, each target VM receives enough linearly independent combinations to decode the entire F bytes by time T. A simple token-bucket scheduler per edge enforces r_{u,v}, and the per-VM cap constraint ensures no VM is asked to exceed its egress limit. Optional helper VMs in non-target regions are included in V when they can serve as cheaper relays; the LP chooses them only when the reduction in edge egress fees outweighs the cost of placing data into them. The complete algorithm therefore outputs both the overlay topology—which VMs send to which VMs and at what average rate—and a concrete store-and-forward chunk schedule, so an engineer can directly launch the VM instances and run the transmission loop.
